title: Iterbench pulse: batcher-window sweep & tail characterization
content:
Quick notes from a light-weight iteration bench (personal scratchpad). Goal: validate the new batching window heuristic (adaptive-window) vs the baseline fixed-window (12ms) on medium bursty load and capture tail behaviors + warmup penalty. Summary/claim: adaptive-window reduced p99 by ~18–22% at 200–500 qps for mixed short/long requests with modest impact on p50. However, we still see discrete tail spikes correlated with collector cycles and occasional kernel wakeups at very low concurrency. Experiment context - node image: rwinf-prod-runtime:v2024-10-29-experiments - model: llama-13b-8bit-q4 (quantized test build) - sequence length: 512 prompt + 256 generation (avg tokens 420) - hardware: 1x A10G, 32GB; pinned to CUDA device 0 - runtime flags: --batcher=adaptive-window --window-min-ms=2 --window-max-ms=20 --max-batch=64 - baseline flags: --batcher=fixed-window --window-ms=12 --max-batch=64 - client: wrk2 (kept arrival rate steady), payloads: mix_short (50% 8 tokens), mix_long (50% 160 tokens) - runs: 3 warm runs + 5 samples each point; each sample = 10m steady phase + 2m cooldown Key commands (repro) - start runtime (adaptive): ./run_server.sh --model=llama-13b-q4 --flags="--batcher adaptive-window --window-min-ms 2 --window-max-ms 20" & - wrk2: wrk2 -t8 -c200 -d600s -R200 --script=payload_mix.lua http://localhost:8080/generate Aggregate numbers (median across samples) - QPS target: 200, 350, 500 Baseline (fixed 12ms): - qps=200: p50=38ms, p95=142ms, p99=312ms, tokens/sec (server)=77k, GPU util=62% - qps=350: p50=53ms, p95=220ms, p99=470ms, tokens/sec=132k, GPU util=78% - qps=500: p50=71ms, p95=320ms, p99=840ms, tokens/sec=186k, GPU util=92% Adaptive-window: - qps=200: p50=41ms, p95=122ms, p99=255ms, tokens/sec=79k, GPU util=65% - qps=350: p50=56ms, p95=185ms, p99=370ms, tokens/sec=136k, GPU util=82% - qps=500: p50=74ms, p95=290ms, p99=690ms, tokens/sec=188k, GPU util=94% Observations: - p99 improvement is consistent across points (18–22% reduction) for adaptive. Biggest win at mid QPS (350). - p50 slightly increases (~5–8ms) under adaptive; likely due to waiting window being slightly larger for coalescing small requests. Tradeoff expected. - tokens/sec and GPU util increased slightly with adaptive (better packing -> higher throughput). - At qps=500 tail still grows (p99 ~690ms) — likely saturation + occasional long kernel wakeups. Need to investigate kernel latencies + driver-level jitter. Tail analysis (traces + sampling) - captured 1s histograms and stack-sampled traces during worst tails. Two dominant patterns: 1) long syscall blocking in NVML driver around GPU memory accounting (20–60ms) — infrequent but visible; correlates with OS-level nv-hostcalls. 2) occasional Python GC pause in the control-plane process when trace/span aggregation spikes (10–40ms). We saw p99 spikes aligned with trace flush intervals. Warmup behavior - cold-to-steady: first 30s show increased p95/p99 (cache misses for KV cache priming + initial CUDA kernel compilation). Adaptive-window slightly worsened the first few seconds for tiny bursts because it lets a few tiny requests wait to fill batches -> measured as larger absolutes. Mitigation: small startup fast-path (window-min-ms=1 for first 45s) seems to help. Notes / hypotheses - Hypothesis A: reduce p99 further by jittering batch release slightly (random between min and computed window) to avoid aligned kernel wakeups. - Hypothesis B: move trace aggregation off the hot path or throttle flushes under load to avoid GC-induced tailing. - Hypothesis C: investigate kernel driver NVML settings or upgrade driver to newer minor that reduces nv-hostcall stalls. Quick TODOs (next local experiments) - [ ] Run adaptive-window + randomized-release (seeded) at qps=350/500 and collect p99 histograms (MUST sample 10m). - [ ] Add controlled stress on trace aggregator: toggle TRACE_LEVEL sampling to mimic prod and measure delta. - [ ] Re-run with --window-max-ms=12 (tighter cap) to measure midpoint tradeoff. - [ ] Create lightweight evict/prime script to pre-warm CUDA kernels before client arrival (warmup helper). Slack references and context - Posted initial numbers in #eng-serving-runtime (thread: "iterbench adaptive window results") — Arjun saw similar on his A40 host but with slightly lower GC noise. - Related PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/392 (adaptive-window proto). - Relevant JIRA: JIRA-ENG-2148 (batcher tuning epic). Misc scribbles (notes-to-self) - watch for too-high window-min (2ms is borderline for low-latency clients). Try 1ms early-fastpath. - consider a hybrid: small-requests shortcut if estimated service latency < 30ms (fastpath). - log-level: enable fine tracing only during tail sampling windows to avoid extra overhead in steady-state. Conclusion (working): adaptive-window looks promising for unit economics (more tokens/sec) and tail reduction across typical burst ranges. Need focused tail-hunting for kernel/GC sources before promoting as default. For next demo to product, prepare a short deck showing p99 reductions + cost-per-token delta.
